claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase FCC matrix in its initial state.
High-temperature degradation of this alloy is governed by selective oxidation of Cr.
Al and Ti make minor contributions to selective oxide formation.
Oxidizing exposure produces a layered oxide scale with a continuous Cr-rich inner layer and a more porous outer layer.
The Cr-rich inner oxide is slow-growing and adherent.
The Cr-rich oxide acts as a protective barrier that retards oxygen ingress along grain-boundary pathways.
The protective oxide barrier minimizes degradation of the underlying FCC matrix during oxidizing exposure.
Formation of the protective scale results in minimal losses of macroscopic strength and fatigue performance.
Reducing exposure produces an incomplete, less-adherent, or discontinuous oxide scale.
Discontinuity of the oxide scale under reducing conditions permits faster degradation than under oxidizing conditions.
The FCC structure will be retained after reducing exposure despite the higher degradation rate.
The as-fabricated baseline has minimal pre-existing oxide scale.
The proposed protective behavior is most significant at 600–900 °C for exposures of 50–120 hours.
Matched oxidizing and reducing exposures followed by microscopy, chemical profiling, and mechanical testing can distinguish the proposed scale-mediated mechanism.
Similar oxide morphologies without a distinct Cr-rich inner layer and comparable mechanical degradation rates in both atmospheres would falsify the hypothesis.
